newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish minister quits over house allegations.
newsitem.headline: Irish minister quits over house allegations.

text.p: Ireland's Transport Minister Michael Lowry resigned on Saturday night after reports that a department store had paid for a 200,000 pound ($320,000) extension at his Tipperary home.
"I am guilty of no impropriety but am going in the interests of the government," Lowry said after a 30-minute meeting with Prime Minister John Bruton.
"The decision is mine and mine alone."

His resignation followed a newspaper report on Friday that Dunnes Stores, an island-wide department store, had paid for the extension at his home in 1993 when he was chairman of Bruton's Fine Gael parliamentary party.
Lowry, 42, said he was resigning to clarify the circumstances surrounding the affair from outside the government, which has to contest a general election before November next year.
He gave no immediate explanation as to why Dunnes had paid for the building work.
Lowry heads a refigeration company, Streamline Enterprises Ltd, which won the contract to provide equipment to Dunnes.
Bruton, who came to power promising a government as "transparent as a pane of glass," said he regretted losing Lowry, who was seen as a rising young star in the party.
Alan Dukes, a 51-year-old former leader of Fine Gael, was named as Lowry's ministerial successor on Saturday night.
The Irish Times said in a front-page report the affair posed the "most serious ethical question of its (the government's) term in office."
The resignation will not directly affect Bruton's parliamentary majority of five, but it is expected to raise further calls from the opposition for an early election after a series of mishaps.
Bruton heads the ruling coalition with two junior parties, the Labour Party and Democratic Left.

The government was deeply embarrassed this month when it came to light that 16 top-security prisoners including IRA guerrilla suspects were released because the judge sitting over their case had been removed from his duties months before.
The 16 were promptly re-arrested and returned to jail to await trial but the opposition said it was a monumental blunder that merited the immediate resignation of all involved.
Justice Minister Nora Owen has resisted calls to resign but her department was accused of bungling in an official probe.

Labour brought down the previous coalition, led by the Fianna Fail party of former prime minister Albert Reynolds, because of a scandal surrounding the failure of the attorney-general to respond to an extradition request from Northern Ireland for a suspected paedophile priest.
